sections.title: Grammatical Gender
sections.rule: Every German noun is masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das), and gender is mostly unpredictable, so learn each noun together with its article. In the plural all genders use die.
sections.example_target: Der Mann, die Frau und das Kind wohnen hier.
sections.example_target_2: Die Kinder spielen im Garten.
sections.example_ref: English: The man, the woman and the child live here. / The children play in the garden.
sections.note: Learn the article WITH the noun (der Tisch, die Lampe, das Buch) — never the noun alone. Endings help: -ung, -heit, -keit are die; -chen, -lein are das.

sections.title: Nominative Case
sections.rule: The nominative marks the subject — who or what does the action — and answers wer? or was? The articles are der/die/das/die and ein/eine/ein.
sections.example_target: Der Hund schläft.
sections.example_target_2: Ein Kind lacht.
sections.example_ref: English: The dog is sleeping. / A child is laughing.
sections.note: The verb sein always takes the nominative on both sides: Das ist ein guter Freund (not einen).

sections.title: Accusative Case
sections.rule: The accusative marks the direct object and answers wen? or was? Only the masculine changes: der→den, ein→einen; feminine, neuter and plural stay the same.
sections.example_target: Ich sehe den Mann.
sections.example_target_2: Wir kaufen einen Tisch und eine Lampe.
sections.example_ref: English: I see the man. / We are buying a table and a lamp.
sections.note: The prepositions durch, für, gegen, ohne, um always take the accusative — memorise them as a block.

sections.title: Dative Case
sections.rule: The dative marks the indirect object (to/for whom) and answers wem? Articles become dem/der/dem/den, and plural nouns add -n.
sections.example_target: Ich gebe dem Kind einen Apfel.
sections.example_target_2: Sie hilft den Kindern.
sections.example_ref: English: I give the child an apple. / She helps the children.
sections.note: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu always take the dative. mit dem Bus, nach der Arbeit, zu Hause.

sections.title: Present Tense
sections.rule: Regular verbs drop -en and add -e/-st/-t/-en/-t/-en for ich/du/er/wir/ihr/sie. Some strong verbs change their stem vowel in du and er/sie/es (fahren→du fährst, lesen→er liest).
sections.example_target: Ich spiele Fußball und du liest ein Buch.
sections.example_target_2: Er fährt nach Berlin.
sections.example_ref: English: I play football and you read a book. / He is driving to Berlin.
sections.note: German has no continuous form: Ich spiele means both 'I play' and 'I am playing'. Learn sein, haben and werden first — they are irregular.

sections.title: The Perfekt Tense
sections.rule: The Perfekt is the normal spoken past: conjugated haben or sein plus the Partizip II at the end. Regular participles are ge-…-t (gemacht), strong ones ge-…-en (gesehen). Verbs of motion or change of state use sein.
sections.example_target: Ich habe Pizza gegessen.
sections.example_target_2: Wir sind nach Hause gegangen.
sections.example_ref: English: I ate / have eaten pizza. / We went home.
sections.note: Use sein for movement and change of state (gehen, kommen, fahren, werden, bleiben, sein). Everything else uses haben.

sections.title: Modal Verbs
sections.rule: The modals können, müssen, wollen, sollen, dürfen and mögen are irregular in the singular and push the main verb, as an infinitive, to the very end of the clause.
sections.example_target: Ich kann heute nicht kommen.
sections.example_target_2: Wir müssen jetzt gehen.
sections.example_ref: English: I cannot come today. / We have to go now.
sections.note: ich möchte (I would like) is the polite form of mögen and is the most useful modal for ordering and requests.

sections.title: Separable Verbs
sections.rule: Many verbs have a stressed prefix (an-, auf-, mit-, zurück-) that splits off in a main clause and jumps to the end, while the conjugated stem stays in position 2. In the Perfekt the ge- sits between prefix and stem (angerufen).
sections.example_target: Ich rufe dich morgen an.
sections.example_target_2: Der Zug fährt um acht Uhr ab.
sections.example_ref: English: I will call you tomorrow. / The train departs at eight o'clock.
sections.note: If you can stress the prefix, it separates (ÁNrufen). Unstressed prefixes (be-, ver-, ent-, er-) never separate: Ich verstehe dich.

sections.title: Genitive Case
sections.rule: The genitive shows possession and answers wessen? Articles become des/der/des/der, and masculine and neuter nouns add -s or -es.
sections.example_target: Das Auto des Mannes ist neu.
sections.example_target_2: Die Farbe der Blumen ist schön.
sections.example_ref: English: The man's car is new. / The colour of the flowers is beautiful.
sections.note: In everyday speech the genitive is often replaced by von + dative: das Auto von meinem Vater. wegen, während, trotz and statt take the genitive.

sections.title: Adjective Endings
sections.rule: An adjective before a noun takes an ending set by gender, case and the article type. After der/die/das it is weak (mostly -e/-en); after ein/kein/mein it is mixed; with no article it is strong and carries the article's signal itself.
sections.example_target: Der gute Wein kommt aus einem kleinen Dorf.
sections.example_target_2: Ich trinke kalten Kaffee mit frischer Milch.
sections.example_ref: English: The good wine comes from a small village. / I drink cold coffee with fresh milk.
sections.note: Rule of thumb: if the article already shows the case (der, dem, den), the adjective just takes -e or -en. With no article, the adjective must show it: guter Wein, kaltes Wasser.

sections.title: Subordinate Clause Word Order
sections.rule: Subordinating conjunctions like weil, dass, wenn and obwohl send the conjugated verb to the very end of their clause. A comma separates the two clauses.
sections.example_target: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin.
sections.example_target_2: Ich weiß, dass er heute kommt.
sections.example_ref: English: I am staying home because I am ill. / I know that he is coming today.
sections.note: If the subordinate clause comes first, the main clause starts with its verb: Weil ich krank bin, bleibe ich zu Hause (verb-comma-verb).

sections.title: Reflexive Verbs & Pronouns
sections.rule: Reflexive verbs use a pronoun that refers back to the subject. Most use the accusative (mich, dich, sich), but when there is already a direct object the reflexive is dative (mir, dir, sich).
sections.example_target: Ich freue mich auf das Wochenende.
sections.example_target_2: Ich wasche mir die Hände.
sections.example_ref: English: I am looking forward to the weekend. / I wash my hands.
sections.note: sich is the same for er/sie/es/Sie/sie(pl). Dative appears when there is a separate object (mir die Hände) — the hands are the object, so the reflexive shifts to dative.

sections.title: Comparative & Superlative
sections.rule: Add -er + als for comparisons and am …-sten (or der/die/das …-ste before a noun) for the superlative. Short vowels a/o/u usually take an umlaut.
sections.example_target: Berlin ist größer als München.
sections.example_target_2: Der Mount Everest ist am höchsten.
sections.example_ref: English: Berlin is bigger than Munich. / Mount Everest is the highest.
sections.note: Learn the irregulars: gut→besser→am besten, viel→mehr→am meisten, gern→lieber→am liebsten, hoch→höher→am höchsten.

sections.title: Passive Voice
sections.rule: The passive uses werden plus the Partizip II. werden is conjugated for the tense (wird/wurde/ist … worden) and the participle goes to the end; the doer, if named, follows von.
sections.example_target: Das Haus wird gebaut.
sections.example_target_2: Der Brief wurde von Anna geschrieben.
sections.example_ref: English: The house is being built. / The letter was written by Anna.
sections.note: In the Perfekt passive the participle of werden is worden, not geworden: Das Haus ist gebaut worden.

sections.title: The Präteritum
sections.rule: The Präteritum is the simple past used in narration and writing. Weak verbs insert -te (machte), strong verbs change the stem (ging, kam, fand). For sein, haben and the modals it is preferred even in speech.
sections.example_target: Es war kalt und ich hatte keine Zeit.
sections.example_target_2: Er ging nach Hause und machte das Licht aus.
sections.example_ref: English: It was cold and I had no time. / He went home and turned off the light.
sections.note: In conversation use the Perfekt for most verbs, but say war, hatte, konnte, wollte rather than the clumsy Perfekt forms.

sections.title: Futur I
sections.rule: The future uses conjugated werden plus an infinitive at the end of the clause. It expresses intentions, predictions and, with wohl, assumptions about the present.
sections.example_target: Ich werde morgen nach Hamburg fahren.
sections.example_target_2: Sie wird das sicher schaffen.
sections.example_ref: English: I will travel to Hamburg tomorrow. / She will surely manage it.
sections.note: Germans often use the present tense with a time word for the future: Morgen fahre ich nach Hamburg. Futur I is mainly for predictions and emphasis.

sections.title: Two-Way Prepositions
sections.rule: The Wechselpräpositionen an, auf, in, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben and zwischen take the accusative for movement toward a goal (wohin?) and the dative for a fixed location (wo?).
sections.example_target: Ich gehe in die Schule.
sections.example_target_2: Ich bin in der Schule.
sections.example_ref: English: I am going into the school. / I am at school.
sections.note: Ask wohin? (motion → accusative) or wo? (position → dative). Verbs like stellen/legen/hängen (put) take accusative; stehen/liegen/hängen (be located) take dative.

sections.title: Relative Clauses
sections.rule: Relative pronouns (der, die, das and forms like dem, den, dessen) agree in gender and number with the noun they describe, but their case comes from their role inside the relative clause, whose verb goes to the end.
sections.example_target: Der Mann, der dort wohnt, ist mein Onkel.
sections.example_target_2: Das Buch, das ich lese, ist spannend.
sections.example_ref: English: The man who lives there is my uncle. / The book that I am reading is exciting.
sections.note: Gender/number come from the main noun; case comes from the job inside the clause. Always fence the clause with commas.

sections.title: Infinitive with zu
sections.rule: Many verbs and expressions are completed by zu plus an infinitive at the end. For purpose use um … zu (in order to). With separable verbs the zu sits inside the verb (anzurufen).
sections.example_target: Es ist wichtig, jeden Tag zu üben.
sections.example_target_2: Ich lerne Deutsch, um in Berlin zu arbeiten.
sections.example_ref: English: It is important to practise every day. / I am learning German in order to work in Berlin.
sections.note: Modals, plus sehen, hören, lassen, never use zu: Ich muss gehen, Ich lasse ihn warten. Everything else usually needs zu.

sections.title: Plusquamperfekt
sections.rule: The past perfect uses the Präteritum of haben or sein (hatte/war) plus the Partizip II. It marks an action finished before another past event, often paired with nachdem.
sections.example_target: Nachdem er gegessen hatte, ging er spazieren.
sections.example_target_2: Sie war schon gegangen, als ich ankam.
sections.example_ref: English: After he had eaten, he went for a walk. / She had already left when I arrived.
sections.note: Choose hatte or war by the same rule as the Perfekt: movement/change-of-state verbs take war (war gegangen), the rest hatte (hatte gegessen).

sections.title: Konjunktiv II
sections.rule: The Konjunktiv II expresses hypotheticals, wishes and politeness. Most verbs use würde + infinitive, but sein, haben, and the modals have their own forms: wäre, hätte, könnte, müsste.
sections.example_target: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich dir helfen.
sections.example_target_2: Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen?
sections.example_ref: English: If I had time, I would help you. / Could you please help me?
sections.note: For polite requests always reach for könnte, hätte gern or würde: Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee is far softer than Ich will einen Kaffee.

sections.title: Konjunktiv I
sections.rule: The Konjunktiv I signals reported (indirect) speech in news and formal writing. It is built from the verb stem plus -e/-est/-e endings; common forms are sei, habe and gehe.
sections.example_target: Er sagt, er sei krank.
sections.example_target_2: Die Ministerin erklärte, sie habe keine Zeit.
sections.example_ref: English: He says he is ill. / The minister stated that she had no time.
sections.note: When the Konjunktiv I looks identical to the present tense, writers switch to Konjunktiv II to keep the reported sense clear: Sie sagen, sie hätten kein Geld.
